chapter: Opinions on playing and old New Orleans
title: Thinking of chords and reading ahead
summary: Foster does not think of chord names; he reads bars ahead and ideas come as he plays.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: When you're playing with the band, do you think of the different chords? Like do you ever think now we're in the, I'm playing a G chord, now I'm going to go to C, now I play F? No, no, no.

I don't think of nothing like that. You don't think of anything like that? I don't even make it. I don't think of nothing like that. Once I was thinking of a chord, you might make a chord this time, you say, well I want to, you'll try another chord and see if it fit. Right? That's the way I do it. See, my eyes just come to me, my eyes just come to me in the bar. See? My eyes just come to me in the bar. A bar, see? Like when I was reading, I used to try to read a bar ahead, two bars ahead. So I can look around, see? You know? Like playing them shoes, it doesn't make you try to read two bars ahead. You look at your music, see? Read two bars ahead and then you get on and you do it and then you grab your two more parts. See? See, when you, see, and when you learn that, your changes come to you, you know what you're going to do. Right. See? But sometimes your ideas come to you so fast, when your ideas come to you, you can't do nothing. See? Your ideas come too fast, your ideas, but the fingers won't stand for the ideas. Right. See?
